proofs.proof_tex:
Iterating the fine recursion \(m\) times gives, for every \(s\in\mathbb Z\),
\[
 X_{ms}=A^mX_{m(s-1)}+\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^r\varepsilon_{ms-r}.
\]
By the definitions of \(Y\), \(B\), and \(\eta\), this is
\[
 Y_s=BY_{s-1}+\eta_s,
 \qquad B=A^m.
\]
The innovation indices entering \(\eta_s\) form the block
\(\{m(s-1)+1,\ldots,ms\}\). These blocks are disjoint for distinct values of
\(s\). Hence \(\mathrm{ass{:}gaussian\mbox{-}innovations}\) implies that the
\(\eta_s\) are independent centered Gaussian vectors. The same block is
strictly later than all innovations measurable with respect to
\(Y_{s-1}\), so \(\eta_s\) is independent of \(Y_{s-1}\). Independence of
the fine innovations also gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(\eta_s)
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top=Q.
\]
Because \(D\succ0\), the term with \(r=0\) shows that \(Q\succ0\).

Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}stable\mbox{-}transition}\) gives
\(\rho(B)=\rho(A)^m<1\). The unique stationary covariance therefore obeys
\[
 M_0=BM_0B^\top+Q.
\]
It is positive definite because
\(M_0=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^kQ(B^k)^\top\succeq Q\succ0\). Taking the
cross-moment of the coarse recursion with \(Y_{s-1}\), and using the
independence just proved, yields
\[
 M_1=\mathbb E[Y_sY_{s-1}^\top]=BM_0.
\]
Thus division by \(M_0\) is legitimate and
\[
 B=M_1M_0^{-1},
 \qquad Q=M_0-BM_0B^\top.
\]

Conversely, let \(B\) be real with \(\rho(B)<1\), and let \(Q\succ0\).
For independent \(N(0,Q)\) vectors \((\eta_s)_{s\in\mathbb Z}\), the series
\[
 Y_s=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k\eta_{s-k}
\]
converges in \(L^2\), since finite-dimensional stability implies a bound
\(\lVert B^k\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le Cc^k\) for some \(C<\infty\) and
\(c<1\). It is the unique stationary solution of
\(Y_s=BY_{s-1}+\eta_s\). Its mean is zero and its covariance sequence is
\[
 \Gamma_0=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^kQ(B^k)^\top,
 \qquad \Gamma_j=B^j\Gamma_0\quad(j\ge0),
\]
with \(\Gamma_{-j}=\Gamma_j^\top\). A centered Gaussian process is determined
by its covariance function, so stable \(B\) and positive definite \(Q\)
determine the entire stationary coarse Gaussian law.

Fix a member of \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max})\).
The lower-triangular restriction and the stability-margin restriction imply
\(\rho(A)=\max_i|A_{ii}|\le1-\gamma<1\), so the coarse-law reduction applies.
Put
\[
 r_0=(1-\gamma)^m,
 \qquad \beta=(dL)^m,
 \qquad
 \overline q=d_{\max}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(dL)^{2r}.
\]
The entry envelope gives
\(\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm F}\le dL\).
Consequently,
\[
 \lVert B\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=\lVert A^m\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le\beta,
 \qquad
 \lVert Q\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le d_{\max}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^{2r}
 \le\overline q.
\]

We next bound the coarse resolvent without assuming that \(B\) is normal.
Write \(B=\Delta+T\), where \(\Delta\) is diagonal and \(T\) is strictly
lower triangular. Since \(\Delta_{ii}=A_{ii}^m\), for every \(|w|=1\),
\[
 \lVert(I-w\Delta)^{-1}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le(1-r_0)^{-1}.
\]
Moreover, \(\beta\ge1\) and
\(\lVert T\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le\lVert B\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}+
\lVert\Delta\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\beta\). The matrix
\(S_w=(I-w\Delta)^{-1}wT\) is strictly lower triangular, hence
\(S_w^d=0\). Factoring \(I-wB=(I-w\Delta)(I-S_w)\) and using the finite
geometric sum gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \lVert(I-wB)^{-1}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 &\le {1\over1-r_0}\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}
 \left({2\beta\over1-r_0}\right)^k
 =:R_B.
 \end{split}
\]

Let \(\Sigma_n=\operatorname{Cov}(W_n)\). The stationary coarse VAR has
matrix spectral density, in the convention in which covariance is the
normalized Fourier integral,
\[
 F_Y(w)=(I-wB)^{-1}Q(I-\overline w B^\top)^{-1},
 \qquad |w|=1.
\]
For any block vector \(c=(c_0^\top,\ldots,c_n^\top)^\top\), the spectral
representation and Parseval's identity yield
\[
 c^\top\Sigma_nc
 \le \sup_{|w|=1}\lVert F_Y(w)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
       \sum_{s=0}^n\lVert c_s\rVert_2^2
 \le \overline q R_B^2\lVert c\rVert_2^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \lVert\Sigma_n\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le \overline q R_B^2
 =d_{\max}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(dL)^{2r}
 \left[
 {1\over1-(1-\gamma)^m}
 \sum_{k=0}^{d-1}
 \left\{{2(dL)^m\over1-(1-\gamma)^m}\right\}^{k}
 \right]^2
 =K_\Sigma.
\]
This calculation also proves explicitly that \(K_\Sigma\) is independent of
the chosen member of the compact class and of \(n\).

For completeness, we verify both the overlap constants and the Gaussian
tail used below. The unique symmetric matrix representing
\((\widehat M_0)_{ij}\) as a quadratic form has \(n\) diagonal time blocks
when \(i=j\), and has the two symmetric entries of size \(1/(2n)\) for each
of the \(n\) products when \(i\ne j\). The symmetric matrix representing
\((\widehat M_1)_{ij}\) has entries \(1/(2n)\) in the two transpose
positions corresponding to each product
\(Y_{s,i}Y_{s-1,j}\). A row contains at most two such lag-one entries.
Therefore, for every \(\ell\in\{0,1\}\) and \(i,j\in V\),
\[
 \lVert H_{\ell ij}\rVert_{\mathrm F}\le n^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 \lVert H_{\ell ij}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le n^{-1}.
\]
The operator bound in the lag-one case follows also from the maximum
absolute row sum; the Frobenius calculation counts the two symmetric
copies, so it already accounts for overlapping observations.

Let \(Z\) be a standard Gaussian vector and let \(C\) be symmetric. After
orthogonal diagonalization, for
\(0<2\theta\lVert C\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}<1\), independence and the scalar
normal moment generating function give
\[
 \log\mathbb E\exp\{\theta(Z^\top CZ-\operatorname{tr}C)\}
 =\sum_a\left[-\theta\lambda_a-\tfrac12\log(1-2\theta\lambda_a)\right]
 \le {\theta^2\lVert C\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2
       \over1-2\theta\lVert C\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}.
\]
Here we used
\(-\log(1-x)-x\le x^2/(2(1-|x|))\) for \(|x|<1\), which follows by
termwise comparison of its power series. Chernoff's inequality, optimized
in \(\theta\), and the same calculation with \(-C\), imply
\[
 \Pr\left\{|Z^\top CZ-\operatorname{tr}C|>
 2\lVert C\rVert_{\mathrm F}\sqrt t+
 2\lVert C\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}t\right\}\le2e^{-t}
 \quad(t>0).
\]

Apply this result with
\(C=\Sigma_n^{1/2}H_{\ell ij}\Sigma_n^{1/2}\). Stationarity gives
\(\mathbb E[W_n^\top H_{\ell ij}W_n]=(M_\ell)_{ij}\), and the preceding
bounds give
\[
 \lVert C\rVert_{\mathrm F}\le K_\Sigma n^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 \lVert C\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le K_\Sigma n^{-1}.
\]
Thus, with \(t=t_\alpha=\log(4d^2/\alpha)>0\),
\[
 \Pr\left\{|(\widehat M_\ell-M_\ell)_{ij}|>r_n\right\}
 \le2e^{-t_\alpha},
 \qquad
 r_n=2K_\Sigma\left\{\sqrt{t_\alpha/n}+t_\alpha/n\right\}.
\]
There are \(2d^2\) indexed entries. The union bound and the definition of
\(t_\alpha\) therefore give
\[
 \Pr\left\{\max_{\ell\in\{0,1\},\,i,j\in V}
 |(\widehat M_\ell-M_\ell)_{ij}|\le r_n\right\}
 \ge1-4d^2e^{-t_\alpha}=1-\alpha.
\]
On this event, each true coordinate belongs to
\([ (\widehat M_\ell)_{ij}-r_n,
    (\widehat M_\ell)_{ij}+r_n ]\). By the defining containment property of
\(\operatorname{Out}_N\), it also belongs to the corresponding rational
outward-rounded interval. Hence
\[
 \Pr\{(M_0,M_1)\in\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\}\ge1-\alpha.
\]
Every bound above is uniform over the compact class, which proves the
claimed uniformity and the assertion that outward rounding cannot reduce
coverage.

Let the true compact-class member be denoted by \((A_\star,D_\star)\), and
let its stationary coarse moments be \((M_{0\star},M_{1\star})\). On the
event
\[
 E_n=\{(M_{0\star},M_{1\star})\in\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\},
\]
the coarse-law reduction gives
\[
 M_{1\star}=A_\star^mM_{0\star},
 \qquad
 M_{0\star}=A_\star^mM_{0\star}(A_\star^m)^\top
 +\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_\star^rD_\star(A_\star^r)^\top.
\]
It also gives \(M_{0\star}\succ0\). Every remaining constraint in the
definition of \(\mathcal R_n\) is exactly one of the triangularity, graph
support, stability-margin, entry-envelope, diagonality, or innovation
eigenvalue conditions defining the compact class. Consequently,
\[
 E_n\subseteq\{(A_\star,D_\star)\in\mathcal R_n\}.
\]
For every \(|z|=1\), the denominator in the transfer is nonzero because
\[
 |1-(A_\star)_{vv}z|\ge1-| (A_\star)_{vv}|
 \ge\gamma>0.
\]
The definition of \(\mathcal C_n^h\) now implies
\[
 E_n\subseteq\{h_{uv}\in\mathcal C_n^h\}.
\]
The uniform moment-box theorem gives \(\Pr(E_n)\ge1-\alpha\), proving the
coverage statement. This argument quantifies over all compatible
\((A,D)\) simultaneously and nowhere chooses a root branch or divides by a
divided difference.

For the noncontraction assertion, suppose two compact-class members
\((A^{(1)},D^{(1)})\) and \((A^{(2)},D^{(2)})\) generate the same moment
pair and satisfy \(h_{uv}^{(1)}\ne h_{uv}^{(2)}\). Repeating the preceding
membership argument for both members shows that on the single event that
their common moment pair lies in the moment box, both transfers lie in
\(\mathcal C_n^h\). In particular, in the supremum norm on
\(\mathbb T\), the diameter is at least
\(\lVert h_{uv}^{(1)}-h_{uv}^{(2)}\rVert_\infty>0\) on an event of
probability at least \(1-\alpha\), for every \(n\).

Such behavior is attained within the stated structural model whenever the
queried arrow \(u\to v\) is allowed by \(G\). Choose
\(0<c<L\), choose \(\lambda\in(d_{\min},d_{\max})\), put
\[
 A^{(1)}=c e_ve_u^\top,
 \qquad A^{(2)}=-c e_ve_u^\top,
 \qquad D^{(1)}=D^{(2)}=\lambda I_d.
\]
Because \(u\ne v\), both transition matrices square to zero. Thus, for every
\(m\ge2\), both models have
\[
 B=0,
 \qquad
 Q=\lambda I_d+\lambda c^2e_ve_v^\top,
\]
and hence the same
\((M_0,M_1)=(Q,0)\), while their transfers are respectively \(cz\) and
\(-cz\). Their diagonal entries vanish, so the stability margin holds; all
support, envelope, positivity, and innovation bounds hold by construction.
This is an explicit interior, transfer-distinct witness to possible
noncontraction.

theorem.statement:
The literal coordinatewise no-wider requirement has a finite-sample valid
fallback. In the spectral-split calibration handle, take the measurable
covariance envelope to be the constant function \(K_\Sigma\), and define
\[
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha)=\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha),
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal R}_n=\mathcal R_n,
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^h=\mathcal C_n^h.
\]
Then every coordinate interval is no wider than its deterministic
\(K_\Sigma\)-box counterpart with probability one, the moment region has
finite-sample coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) uniformly over the compact
class, and the rational encoding and exact semialgebraic inverse are
preserved. This construction certifies equality of widths; the frozen
handle is not used here to claim a strict adaptive improvement.
theorem.proof_tex:
Every real symmetric lag-form matrix has the spectral decomposition
\(H_{\ell ij}=H_{\ell ij}^{+}-H_{\ell ij}^{-}\), where both summands are
positive semidefinite and have orthogonal ranges. Define the proposed
data-measurable covariance envelope by
\(\widehat K_{\Sigma,n}^{+}(W_n)=K_\Sigma\) for every \(W_n\). Bounding the
positive and negative parts by this common envelope and recombining them
recovers exactly the two-sided Gaussian quadratic-form calculation used in
the uniform moment-box theorem. Thus the displayed construction is a
valid, explicit instance of the spectral-split handle, albeit a
non-adaptive fallback.

By construction,
\(\widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha)=\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\) for every
sample. Hence corresponding coordinate widths are equal, so the requested
no-wider with probability tending to one property holds in fact with
probability one for every \(n\). The uniform moment-box theorem gives
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}}
 P\{(M_0,M_1)\in\widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha)\}
 \ge1-\alpha.
\]
Every endpoint remains an output of \(\operatorname{Out}_N\), hence is
rational. The inverse and transfer sets are unchanged, so their defining
polynomial equalities and inequalities, and therefore their exact
semialgebraic inversion, are also unchanged. The global honest-inversion
theorem supplies the corresponding transfer coverage.

Finally, the only formal property used for \(\operatorname{Out}_N(x,r)\)
is containment of \([x-r,x+r]\). The argument proves equality of widths and
makes no assertion of strict width reduction. This does not weaken any of
the three asserted properties, each of which has been verified directly.

For every data-generating member of
\(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max})\),
\(\Pr\{h_{uv}\in\mathcal C_n^h\}\ge1-\alpha\). The claim holds without
selecting a matrix-root branch and without divided-difference or
branch-separation assumptions. If an observed moment law has two compatible
members of the compact class with unequal queried transfers, then the set
need not contract: whenever the common moment pair is in
\(\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\), both attained transfers belong to
\(\mathcal C_n^h\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The coverage and noncontraction clauses are proved, but the unconditional local root-\(n\) diameter clause is too strong under the frozen definition of \(\operatorname{Out}_N\). That definition requires only containment and permits, for example, the valid rational output \( [\lfloor x-r\rfloor-1,\lceil x+r\rceil+1]\), whose excess width does not vanish. A root-\(n\) local diameter requires an additional rounding-excess condition or a precision schedule, neither of which is declared. The proposed claim removes only that unsupported ancillary rate clause.

proofs.proof_tex:
By assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}lower\mbox{-}triangular}\), a nonzero summand in the product expansion of \((A^m)_{vu}\) is indexed by a nondecreasing walk
\[
 u=i_0\le i_1\le\cdots\le i_m=v,
 \qquad
 \prod_{s=1}^{m}A_{i_s i_{s-1}}.
\]
If this walk has exactly one strict increase, that increase must be \(u<v\).  If it occurs between positions \(s\) and \(s+1\), with \(s\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\), its monomial is
\[
 A_{vv}^{m-1-s}A_{vu}A_{uu}^{s}.
\]
Summing these \(m\) monomials and reindexing gives
\[
 A_{vu}\sum_{s=0}^{m-1}A_{vv}^{m-1-s}A_{uu}^{s}
 =A_{vu}C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu}).
\]
Every remaining nonzero walk has at least two strict increases.  Its strict increases give vertices
\[
 u=j_0<j_1<\cdots<j_k=v,
 \qquad k\ge2.
\]
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}graph\mbox{-}support}\), together with the supplied order in \(\mathrm{ass{:}supplied\mbox{-}labeled\mbox{-}order}\), implies that every strict factor \(A_{j_rj_{r-1}}\) follows the directed edge \(j_{r-1}\to j_r\) in \(G\).  Since \(k\ge2\), every such factor satisfies
\[
 0<j_r-j_{r-1}<v-u.
\]
The sum of precisely these remaining monomials is the polynomial \(R_{vu,m}(A)\) from its definition.  Partitioning the complete product expansion into the one-jump and at-least-two-jump walks proves both the displayed identity and the asserted support and endpoint-gap properties.

First suppose \(x\ne y\).  The finite geometric identity gives
\[
 C_m(x,y)=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}x^r y^{m-1-r}
 =\frac{x^m-y^m}{x-y}.
\]
If \(x=y\), direct substitution gives
\[
 C_m(x,x)=m x^{m-1}.
\]
Let \(m\) be odd.  The function \(t\mapsto t^m\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb R\), so, for \(x\ne y\), the numerator \(x^m-y^m\) and denominator \(x-y\) have the same sign.  Hence \(C_m(x,y)>0\).  For \(x=y\ne0\), the integer \(m-1\) is even, and therefore \(m x^{m-1}>0\).  At \((x,y)=(0,0)\), every monomial in the defining sum is zero because \(m-1\ge1\), so \(C_m(0,0)=0\).

Now let \(m\) be even.  When \(x\ne y\), the quotient above vanishes exactly when \(x^m=y^m\), equivalently \(|x|=|y|\); the inequality \(x\ne y\) then makes this equivalent to \(x=-y\).  When \(x=y\), the value \(m x^{m-1}\) vanishes exactly when \(x=0\), which again is exactly the coincident case of \(x=-y\).  Conversely, substituting \(y=-x\) in the defining sum, including \(x=0\), gives zero.  This proves both zero-set assertions.

Let \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  Because a triangular matrix and each of its powers have diagonal entries equal to the corresponding powers of the original diagonal entries,
\[
 B_{ii}=(A^m)_{ii}=A_{ii}^m.
\]
The map \(x\mapsto x^m\) is one-to-one on \(\mathbb R\) for odd \(m\), so necessarily
\[
 A_{ii}=B_{ii}^{1/m}
\]
for every \(i\).  Thus every compatible pair has the same diagonal transition coefficients.

Proceed by induction on the endpoint gap \(g=i-j\ge1\).  All entries of gap zero have just been determined.  Suppose all allowed entries of gap less than \(g\) have been determined.  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}path\mbox{-}expansion}\) gives, for an allowed edge \(j\to i\) of gap \(g\),
\[
 B_{ij}=A_{ij}C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})+R_{ij,m}(A).
\]
Every off-diagonal factor in \(R_{ij,m}(A)\) has gap less than \(g\), so the induction hypothesis determines the remainder.  By the hypothesis on allowed edges and Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}divided\mbox{-}difference\mbox{-}zero\mbox{-}set}\),
\[
 C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})>0.
\]
Division is therefore valid and forces
\[
 A_{ij}=\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)}{C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})}.
\]
For a forbidden pair, graph support forces \(A_{ij}=0\), and the same path expansion turns the equality \(A^m=B\) at that coordinate into the check \(B_{ij}=R_{ij,m}(A)\).  Induction over \(g=1,\ldots,d-1\) proves that there is at most one graph-compatible \(A\) and gives the asserted recursion.

Fix this \(A\).  Since \(D\) is diagonal, the \((i,i)\) entry of the coarse covariance equation is
\[
 Q_{ii}
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{d}D_{jj}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}.
\]
Lower triangularity gives \((A^r)_{ij}=0\) for \(j>i\), while \((A^r)_{ii}=A_{ii}^r\).  Hence
\[
 Q_{ii}
 =D_{ii}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}
  +\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}.
\]
The coefficient of \(D_{ii}\) is at least its \(r=0\) term, namely one.  Starting at \(i=1\) and increasing \(i\), division therefore uniquely yields exactly the displayed innovation recursion.  Thus there is at most one diagonal \(D\).

For sufficiency, construct \(A\) and \(D\) by these recursions.  The diagonal and allowed-coordinate equations for \(A^m=B\) hold by construction; imposing the forbidden-coordinate checks gives the full equation \(A^m=B\).  The diagonal covariance equations hold by construction; imposing the remaining entries gives the full equation \(Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top\).  The graph zeros are built into \(A\).  The explicit stability and positivity checks give \(\max_i|A_{ii}|<1\) and diagonal \(D\succ0\), respectively.  These are precisely all conditions in \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\), proving sufficiency.  Necessity of each check follows immediately from the definition of that fiber.  It follows that every nonempty fiber is a singleton.

Finally, \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is the image of the compatible fiber under
\[
 (A,D)\longmapsto \left[z\longmapsto\frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}\right].
\]
Stability gives \(|A_{vv}z|<1\) for \(|z|=1\), so the denominator never vanishes.  The singleton parameter fiber therefore maps to the singleton containing the causal transfer \(h_{uv}\), rather than defining that causal transfer from the observed law.

For an exact two-node stress test satisfying the regularity condition, take \(m=3\),
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\1/4&1/3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad D=I_2.
\]
Then \(B_{11}=1/8\), \(B_{22}=1/27\), and, since there is no indirect path,
\[
 B_{21}=\frac14 C_3(1/3,1/2)
 =\frac14\left(\frac19+\frac16+\frac14\right)=\frac{19}{144}.
\]
The formula recovers \(A_{21}=(19/144)/(19/36)=1/4\), and the covariance recursion recovers both entries of \(D=I_2\), so the recovered transfer is \(z/[4(1-z/3)]\).  The excluded condition is load-bearing: with
\[
 A(a)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\a&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 D(a)=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2-a^2q_1),
\]
where \(q_1,q_2>0\) and \(|a|<\sqrt{q_2/q_1}\), one has \(A(a)^3=0\) and
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{2}A(a)^rD(a)(A(a)^r)^\top
 =\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2).
\]
Thus the same coarse law admits an open interval of transfers \(az\) when both endpoint persistences vanish.

Use one variable for every graph-allowed lower-triangular entry of \(A\) and one variable \(d_i\) for every diagonal entry of \(D\).  The compatible fiber is the realization of the following finite semialgebraic system over \(K\):
\[
 A^m-B=0,\qquad
 \sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top-Q=0,\qquad
 -1<A_{ii}<1,\qquad d_i>0,
\]
together with the fixed graph-zero equations and \(D_{ij}=0\) for \(i\ne j\).  All matrix powers and covariance entries are polynomials in these finitely many variables.  Because \(A\) is triangular, the strict diagonal inequalities are equivalent to \(\rho(A)<1\), and because \(D\) is diagonal, the inequalities \(d_i>0\) are equivalent to \(D\succ0\).  Thus this semialgebraic realization is exactly \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\), with neither closure nor endpoint points added.

The diagonal equations are \(A_{ii}^m=B_{ii}\).  There is one real root when \(m\) is odd and zero, one, or two real roots when \(m\) is even, so the certificate has finitely many diagonal branches.  On a branch, Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}path\mbox{-}expansion}\) expresses each coordinate in increasing endpoint gap as
\[
 A_{ij}C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})=B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A).
\]
Whenever the displayed coefficient is nonzero, exact division eliminates \(A_{ij}\); when it is zero, the coordinate and its polynomial equation remain in the residual system.  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}divided\mbox{-}difference\mbox{-}zero\mbox{-}set}\) decides which case holds on each isolated diagonal branch.  Clearing only products of denominators already constrained to be nonzero preserves equivalence.  The certificate then retains every unused transition equation, every graph-zero equation, every covariance equation, and every strict stability and positivity inequality.  Consequently the finite union of its residual systems has realization exactly \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).

Apply Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}effective\mbox{-}cad\mbox{-}decision\mbox{-}sampling}\) to these residual systems.  It terminates and reports all of them empty if and only if \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=\varnothing\).  This proves the incompatibility branch and its soundness and completeness.

Suppose now that the fiber is nonempty.  Write
\[
 p=A_{vu},\quad q=A_{vv},\qquad
 p'=A'_{vu},\quad q'=A'_{vv}.
\]
Stability ensures that \(1-qz\) and \(1-q'z\) are nonzero on \(\mathbb T\).  The two transfers are identical rational functions if and only if cross multiplication gives the polynomial identity
\[
 p(1-q'z)=p'(1-qz).
\]
Equality of the constant and linear coefficients is equivalent to
\[
 p=p',\qquad pq'=p'q.
\]
Therefore they are unequal exactly when
\[
 (p-p')^2+(pq'-p'q)^2>0.
\]
This test correctly treats the zero-edge case: all pairs \((0,q)\) give the same zero transfer even if their second coordinates differ.

Form a two-copy semialgebraic system by taking two copies of the complete compatible-fiber constraints and adjoining the last strict inequality.  The CAD sampling lemma decides its feasibility.  If feasible, its exact sample consists of two attained points of the original strict fiber and hence gives the two stable transfer-distinct witnesses asserted in the theorem.  If infeasible, every two compatible points have equal transfers.  A sample from the nonempty one-copy system then supplies their common rational function; if its numerator is zero the output is canonically the zero function.  Thus the singleton-transfer and ambiguity outputs are both sound and complete.

No step replaces a strict inequality by a weak one or assumes a zero-dimensional realization.  Hence zero diagonal roots, open and positive-dimensional fibers, and branch mergers remain covered.  As exact destructive checks, take \(d=2,m=3,B=0,Q=I_2\).  The two interior points
\[
 A_{\pm}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ \pm1/2&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad D_{\pm}=\operatorname{diag}(1,3/4)
\]
both satisfy the complete fiber constraints and have transfers \(\pm z/2\), so the two-copy system is feasible and the certificate cannot return a singleton or an endpoint-only artifact.  For \(d=2,m=2\), any compatible point with \(A_{21}\ne0\) has a second compatible point \((-A,D)\): evenness gives \((-A)^m=A^m\), and each covariance summand is unchanged because
\[
 (-A)^rD((-A)^r)^\top=A^rD(A^r)^\top.
\]
The ambiguity inequality has first term \((2A_{21})^2>0\), so the certificate necessarily retains this global sign pair.

Fix a diagonal-root branch, so every \(A_{ii}\) is fixed by \(A_{ii}^m=B_{ii}\).  Process off-diagonal pairs in increasing endpoint gap.  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}path\mbox{-}expansion}\) shows that at an allowed edge \(j\to i\) the only coefficient multiplying the as-yet-undetermined coordinate \(A_{ij}\) is \(C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})\), while its remainder uses only previously processed gaps.  Thus recursion can fail only when this coefficient vanishes.

For odd \(m\), Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}divided\mbox{-}difference\mbox{-}zero\mbox{-}set}\) gives
\[
 C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 A_{ii}=A_{jj}=0.
\]
Taking the union over the finitely many allowed edges proves the first containment.  Each component \(\{A_{ii}=A_{jj}=0\}\) is the common zero set of two coordinate polynomials and is proper; a finite union of these components is also proper, with the empty union allowed when \(G\) has no edges.

For even \(m\), on any fixed real diagonal branch the same lemma gives
\[
 C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 A_{ii}+A_{jj}=0.
\]
This proves the second containment, and every component is a proper algebraic hyperplane.  Outside the relevant union, every division in the increasing-gap recursion is legal.  Induction on the gap therefore determines at most one graph-compatible \(A\) on that diagonal branch; forbidden entries remain fixed at zero and their power equations are checks rather than additional choices.

For a recursively determined \(A\), diagonal \(D\) must obey, for each \(i\),
\[
 Q_{ii}=D_{ii}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}
 +\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}.
\]
The coefficient of \(D_{ii}\) contains the term one and is therefore strictly positive.  Increasing \(i\) consequently determines at most one diagonal \(D\).  The remaining entries of \(A^m=B\), the full covariance equation, strict stability, and positivity of \(D\) can only retain or reject the candidate; they introduce no further candidate on the fixed branch.  This proves the asserted generic phase statement in fine-parameter space, without making any claim that its image complement in observed-law space is algebraic or null.

Let \(\vartheta=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(M_0,M_1)\) and \(\widehat\vartheta=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(\widehat M_0,\widehat M_1)\).  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}uniform\mbox{-}gaussian\mbox{-}lag\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}clt}\) gives the uniform Gaussian limit
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta)\ \Longrightarrow\ N(0,\Omega)
\]
and a uniformly consistent parametric estimate \(\widehat\Omega\).

The population moment map satisfies
\[
 B=M_1M_0^{-1},\qquad Q=M_0-BM_0B^\top.
\]
Indeed \(M_1=\mathbb E[(BY_{s-1}+\eta_s)Y_{s-1}^\top]=BM_0\), because \(\eta_s\) is independent of \(Y_{s-1}\), and the stationary Lyapunov equation gives the formula for \(Q\).  Since \(M_0\succeq d_{\min}I_d\), matrix inversion and these two maps are continuously differentiable on a common neighborhood of all population moments.

On the odd branch, the diagonal root equation is \(B_{ii}=A_{ii}^m\).  The added separation condition gives
\[
 \left|\frac{\partial B_{ii}}{\partial A_{ii}}\right|
 =m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\ge\kappa,
\]
so the inverse diagonal-root map is continuously differentiable with uniformly bounded derivative.  At every allowed off-diagonal coordinate, the regular-class condition gives
\[
 |C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\ge\kappa.
\]
The path expansion shows that its remainder uses only earlier coordinates.  Induction over endpoint gap therefore makes every recursively recovered entry of \(A\) a continuously differentiable function of \(B\) on a common neighborhood, with uniformly bounded first derivative and uniformly vanishing Taylor remainder.  The innovation recursion has denominators
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}\ge1,
\]
so the recovered diagonal \(D\) is likewise a smooth function of \((B,Q)\), although the focal transfer uses only \(A_{vu}\) and \(A_{vv}\).

For \(|z|=1\), the stability margin yields
\[
 |1-A_{vv}z|\ge1-|A_{vv}|\ge\gamma.
\]
Thus the coefficient-pair-to-transfer map is continuously differentiable uniformly over the finite nonempty grid, and direct differentiation gives
\[
 \mathrm dh_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{z}{1-A_{vv}z}\,\mathrm dA_{vu}
 +\frac{A_{vu}z^2}{(1-A_{vv}z)^2}\,\mathrm dA_{vv}.
\]
Let \(J_h\) be the Jacobian of the composite map from \(\vartheta\) to the stacked real and imaginary parts of \((h_{uv}(z))_{z\in\mathcal Z}\).  The uniform Taylor expansion and the preceding moment CLT give
\[
 \sqrt n\,\operatorname{vec}_{\mathbb R}
 \big((\widehat h_{uv}(z)-h_{uv}(z))_{z\in\mathcal Z}\big)
 =J_h\sqrt n(\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta)+o_{\mathbb P}(1)
 \Longrightarrow N(0,\Sigma_h),
\]
uniformly, where
\[
 \Sigma_h=J_h\Omega J_h^\top.
\]
The recursively evaluated Jacobian \(\widehat J_h\) is uniformly consistent, so
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_h=\widehat J_h\widehat\Omega\widehat J_h^\top
 \longrightarrow\Sigma_h
\]
uniformly in probability.

It remains to justify exact nominal simultaneous coverage despite possible correlation or rank deficiency across frequencies.  The contemporaneous and conventional lagged denominator moment matrices differ exactly by
\[
 n^{-1}(Y_nY_n^\top-Y_0Y_0^\top)=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1})
\]
uniformly.  Smoothness of inversion therefore makes their coefficient estimators differ by \(O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1})\), and the displayed estimator has the first-order expansion
\[
 \sqrt n\,\operatorname{vec}(\widehat B-B)
 =\operatorname{vec}\!\left(n^{-1/2}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\eta_sY_{s-1}^\top M_0^{-1}\right)+o_{\mathbb P}(1),
\]
whose covariance is positive definite and uniformly bounded away from zero because \(Q\succeq d_{\min}I_d\) and \(M_0\) is uniformly bounded above.  Since \(u\to v\in G\), the recursive derivative of \(A_{vu}\) with respect to \(B_{vu}\) is \(1/C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})\ne0\).  Moreover, \(|A_{ii}|\le1-\gamma<1\) gives \(|C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})|\le m\), so the absolute value of this derivative is at least \(1/m\).  The diagonal coefficient \(A_{vv}\) depends on \(B_{vv}\), not on \(B_{vu}\).  Also, for every \(z\in\mathcal Z\),
\[
 \left|\frac{\partial h_{uv}(z)}{\partial A_{vu}}\right|
 =\frac{1}{|1-A_{vv}z|}\ge\frac{1}{1+|A_{vv}|}\ge\frac12.
\]
Hence the limiting Gaussian transfer vector is not identically zero, uniformly over the compact subfamily, even when \(A_{vu}=0\) or \(\Sigma_h\) is singular across coordinates.

For a real vector stacked in complex pairs, define
\[
 \|x\|_{\mathcal Z,\infty}
 =\max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt{x_{\Re,z}^2+x_{\Im,z}^2}.
\]
If \(Z_{\Sigma}\sim N(0,\Sigma)\), let \(c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma)\) be the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of \(\|Z_{\Sigma}\|_{\mathcal Z,\infty}\).  On every nonzero Gaussian support subspace this norm has a continuous distribution on \((0,\infty)\) and no atom at zero.  Compactness, the uniform lower nondegeneracy just proved, and a subsequence argument make this continuity uniform over the covariance family.  Consequently
\[
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}=c_{1-\alpha}(\widehat\Sigma_h)
 \longrightarrow c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_h)
\]
uniformly in probability, and the uniform Gaussian approximation gives
\[
 \sup_{(A,D)}\left|
 \Pr\!\left\{
 \max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt n\,|\widehat h_{uv}(z)-h_{uv}(z)|
 \le\widehat c_{1-\alpha}
 \right\}-(1-\alpha)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\]
The event inside this probability is exactly simultaneous membership of every \(h_{uv}(z)\) in the disks stated in the theorem, which proves the claimed Wald coverage.

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(K\) be an effective real closed field.  For every finite Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and strict or weak polynomial inequalities with coefficients in \(K\), cylindrical algebraic decomposition terminates, decides whether its realization in a finite-dimensional affine space is empty, and, when it is nonempty, returns an exact represented sample point.  This decision-and-sampling conclusion applies to open and positive-dimensional semialgebraic realizations as well as to zero-dimensional ones.

added_lemmas.statement:
For fixed \(d,m,G\), uniformly over \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa)\), the vector
\[
 \sqrt n\,\operatorname{vec}_{s}\!\left(\widehat M_0-M_0,\widehat M_1-M_1\right)
\]
converges to a centered Gaussian vector with covariance \(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Cov}(g_0,g_k)\), where \(g_s=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(Y_sY_s^\top-M_0,Y_sY_{s-1}^\top-M_1)\) and \(\operatorname{vec}_{s}\) stacks the distinct lag-zero entries and all lag-one entries.  The covariance series converges absolutely and uniformly.  On the event that \(\widehat B\) is stable, substituting \((\widehat B,\widehat M_0)\) into the Gaussian Isserlis covariance series and projecting the resulting symmetric matrix onto the positive-semidefinite cone gives a uniformly consistent estimator of this long-run covariance; defining it arbitrarily off that event does not affect consistency.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Iterating the fine-grid recursion over one observed interval gives
\[
 Y_s=BY_{s-1}+\eta_s,\qquad
 B=A^m,\qquad
 \eta_s=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^r\varepsilon_{ms-r}.
\]
The innovation blocks are disjoint across \(s\), so the Gaussian-innovation assumption gives independent centered Gaussian \(\eta_s\) with
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(\eta_s)=Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top.
\]
The term \(r=0\) and the innovation bounds imply \(Q\succeq d_{\min}I_d\); the entry envelope, fixed \(d,m\), and \(D\preceq d_{\max}I_d\) give a finite uniform upper bound on \(\|Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}\).

Because \(A\) is lower triangular and \(\max_i|A_{ii}|\le1-\gamma\), the diagonal of \(B\) is bounded by \(\rho_0=(1-\gamma)^m<1\).  Expanding powers of a fixed-dimensional triangular matrix shows that each entry of \(B^k\) is bounded by a constant times \((k+1)^{d-1}\rho_0^{\max(k-d+1,0)}\), uniformly under the entry envelope.  Choosing any \(\rho\in(\rho_0,1)\) absorbs the polynomial factor, and hence there is a finite \(C\), depending only on the displayed class constants, such that
\[
 \sup_{(A,D)}\|B^k\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\rho^k,\qquad k\ge0.
\]
Stationarity now yields
\[
 M_0=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}B^jQ(B^j)^\top,\qquad
 M_1=BM_0.
\]
Consequently \(M_0\succeq Q\succeq d_{\min}I_d\), \(\|M_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) is uniformly bounded, and the lag covariance
\[
 \Gamma_r=\mathbb E(Y_sY_{s-r}^\top)
 =B^rM_0\quad(r\ge0),\qquad \Gamma_{-r}=\Gamma_r^\top,
\]
decays uniformly geometrically.

Index a coordinate of \(g_s\) by \((a,b,\ell)\), where \(\ell\in\{0,1\}\), and write
\[
 \xi_s^{a b\ell}=Y_{s,a}Y_{s-\ell,b}-\mathbb E(Y_{s,a}Y_{s-\ell,b}).
\]
Isserlis' identity for four centered jointly Gaussian variables, obtained by summing the three pairings and cancelling the within-product pairing, gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(\xi_0^{ab\ell},\xi_k^{cd\ell'})
 =\Gamma_{-k,ac}\Gamma_{-\ell-k+\ell',bd}
  +\Gamma_{\ell'-k,ad}\Gamma_{-\ell-k,bc}.
\]
The geometric bound on \(\Gamma_r\) makes the sum over \(k\in\mathbb Z\) absolutely and uniformly convergent, coordinate by coordinate.  It also shows directly that the covariance of the normalized partial sum converges uniformly to that series, because
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{s,t=1}^{n}\operatorname{Cov}(g_s,g_t)
 =\sum_{|k|<n}\left(1-\frac{|k|}{n}\right)\operatorname{Cov}(g_0,g_k),
\]
up to the harmless fixed endpoint convention in the lag-one coordinates.

It remains to establish Gaussianity rather than only covariance convergence.  Fix a real vector \(a\) of matching dimension and stack \((Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)\) into \(\mathbf Y_n\), whose block covariance matrix is \(\Sigma_n\).  The summability of \(\Gamma_r\) implies \(\sup_n\|\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty\).  There is a symmetric block-banded matrix \(H_{n,a}\), with uniformly bounded operator norm and \(\|H_{n,a}\|_{\mathrm F}=O(\sqrt n)\), such that
\[
 a^\top n^{-1/2}\sum_{s=1}^{n}g_s
 =n^{-1/2}\{\mathbf Y_n^\top H_{n,a}\mathbf Y_n-\operatorname{tr}(H_{n,a}\Sigma_n)\}.
\]
Writing \(\mathbf Y_n=\Sigma_n^{1/2}Z_n\) with standard Gaussian \(Z_n\), put
\[
 T_{n,a}=n^{-1/2}\Sigma_n^{1/2}H_{n,a}\Sigma_n^{1/2}.
\]
Uniformly over the class, \(\|T_{n,a}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(n^{-1/2})\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(T_{n,a}^2)=O(1)\).  For fixed real \(t\), diagonalizing \(T_{n,a}\) gives the exact characteristic function
\[
 \mathbb E\exp\{it(Z_n^\top T_{n,a}Z_n-\operatorname{tr}T_{n,a})\}
 =\exp\left\{-it\operatorname{tr}T_{n,a}-\frac12\log\det(I-2itT_{n,a})\right\}.
\]
Expanding the logarithm is valid uniformly for all sufficiently large \(n\), and the linear term cancels, leaving
\[
 -t^2\operatorname{tr}(T_{n,a}^2)+O\!\left(|t|^3\|T_{n,a}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\operatorname{tr}(T_{n,a}^2)\right)
 =-\frac{t^2}{2}a^\top\Omega a+o(1),
\]
where \(\Omega=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Cov}(g_0,g_k)\).  The remainder is uniform.  Taking \(a=t\) and scalar Fourier argument one gives, for every multivariate argument \(t\), uniform convergence of the joint characteristic function to \(\exp(-t^\top\Omega t/2)\).  Uniform boundedness of the second moments gives tightness.  To see directly that this implies uniform weak convergence, truncate a bounded Lipschitz test function to a common compact ball, convolve the truncation with a Gaussian kernel, use Fourier inversion and the just-proved characteristic-function convergence for the convolution, and then let the kernel variance tend to zero and the ball radius tend to infinity.  This proves the stated uniform Gaussian limit, allowing singular \(\Omega\).

Finally, the empirical moments have variance \(O(n^{-1})\) uniformly by the same covariance summability.  Since \(M_0\succeq d_{\min}I_d\), this implies
\[
 \widehat M_0\longrightarrow M_0,\qquad
 \widehat B=\widehat M_1\widehat M_0^{-1}\longrightarrow B
\]
uniformly in probability.  A fixed neighborhood of the compact set of \(B\)'s is stable and obeys a common geometric power bound, so the stable event has probability tending to one uniformly.  Substitute
\[
 \widehat\Gamma_r=\widehat B^r\widehat M_0\quad(r\ge0),\qquad
 \widehat\Gamma_{-r}=\widehat\Gamma_r^\top
\]
into the displayed Isserlis formula and sum over \(k\in\mathbb Z\).  Uniform geometric domination and continuity of each finite partial sum yield consistency by a finite-head plus uniformly small-tail argument.  Symmetrize this estimate and project it onto the closed convex cone of positive-semidefinite matrices.  Since the true long-run covariance belongs to that cone, metric projection cannot increase its Frobenius distance from the truth.  The projected estimate is therefore also uniformly consistent and always defines a Gaussian covariance.  An arbitrary definition on the vanishing-probability unstable event leaves that conclusion unchanged.

Let \(m\) be even.  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}known\mbox{-}sampling\mbox{-}factor}\), \(m\) is the fixed subsampling factor and \(m\geq 2\), so there is an integer \(k\geq 1\) such that \(m=2k\).  Fix \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\), and put \(\widetilde A=-A\).  The defining equalities in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) first give
\[
 \widetilde A^{,m}=(-A)^{2k}=A^{2k}=A^m=B.
\]
For every \(r\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\), scalar multiplication commutes with matrix powers and transposition, whence
\[
 \widetilde A^{,r}D(\widetilde A^{,r})^\top
 =(-1)^rA^rD\bigl((-1)^rA^r\bigr)^\top
 =(-1)^{2r}A^rD(A^r)^\top
 =A^rD(A^r)^\top.
\]
Summation and the covariance equality in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) therefore yield
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\widetilde A^{,r}D(\widetilde A^{,r})^\top
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top
 =Q.
\]
All zero restrictions are preserved because \(\widetilde A_{ij}=-A_{ij}\): in particular, \(\widetilde A_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i<j\), and also whenever \(i>j\) but \(j\to i\notin G\).  The diagonal stability restriction is preserved since
\[
 \max_i|\widetilde A_{ii}|=\max_i|-A_{ii}|=\max_i|A_{ii}|<1.
\]
Finally, \(D\) is unchanged, so it remains diagonal and positive definite.  These checks exhaust the defining constraints of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\); hence
\[
 (-A,D)=(\widetilde A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G).
\]

For completeness, the equality just proved is equality of the full stationary coarse Gaussian laws, not only equality of two displayed parameters.  For \(s\in\{1,-1\}\), set \(A_s=sA\), take an independent sequence \((\varepsilon_t^{(s)})_{t\in\mathbb Z}\) with law \(N(0,D)\), and form the stationary Gaussian recursion
\[
 X_t^{(s)}=A_sX_{t-1}^{(s)}+\varepsilon_t^{(s)}.
\]
This stationary process exists because \(A_s\) is triangular and
\(\rho(A_s)=\max_i|(A_s)_{ii}|<1\); explicitly, the series
\(X_t^{(s)}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}A_s^\ell\varepsilon_{t-\ell}^{(s)}\)
converges in second mean.  Iterating the recursion over one sampling block and writing \(Y_j^{(s)}=X_{jm}^{(s)}\) gives
\[
 Y_j^{(s)}=A_s^mY_{j-1}^{(s)}+\eta_j^{(s)},
 \qquad
 \eta_j^{(s)}=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_s^r\varepsilon_{jm-r}^{(s)}.
\]
Different \(j\)'s use disjoint innovation blocks, so the variables \(\eta_j^{(s)}\) are independent; they are centered Gaussian and independent of the preceding coarse history.  The two calculations above imply, for both signs \(s\),
\[
 A_s^m=B,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}(\eta_j^{(s)})
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_s^rD(A_s^r)^\top=Q.
\]
Moreover \(\rho(B)=\rho(A)^m<1\), so the stationary covariance of either coarse process is the convergent series
\[
 \Gamma_0=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}B^\ell Q(B^\ell)^\top.
\]
Thus both sampled processes have the same stationary initial law \(N(0,\Gamma_0)\), the same transition matrix \(B\), and independent innovations with the same law \(N(0,Q)\).  Recursive conditioning therefore gives equality of all their finite-dimensional distributions.  This proves the asserted same-law property even after the complete coarse covariance restriction is imposed.

It remains to show that the same law can carry two different queried transfers.  The assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}query\mbox{-}edge}\) fixes \(u\to v\) as the queried process-DAG arrow.  Write \(p=A_{vu}\) and \(q=A_{vv}\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}transfer\mbox{-}fiber}\), the points \((A,D)\) and \((-A,D)\) found above contribute, respectively,
\[
 h_+(z)=\frac{pz}{1-qz}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 h_-(z)=\frac{-pz}{1+qz}
\]
to \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\).  Since \(|q|<1\), both denominators are nonzero for every \(z\in\mathbb T\).  If these rational functions were equal, cross-multiplication would give the polynomial identity
\[
 pz(1+qz)=-pz(1-qz),
 \qquad\text{and hence}\qquad
 2pz=0.
\]
This is impossible when \(p=A_{vu}\neq0\).  Consequently \(h_+\neq h_-\), and both are attained elements of the same transfer fiber.  That fiber is therefore not a singleton.  Because the two compatible Gaussian structural models induce exactly the same observed coarse law, no functional of that law can equal the nonzero queried fine-grid transfer in both models; point identification fails.

Work under the queried-edge hypothesis and the effective-input hypothesis.  Since \(d=2\), the ordered vertex set is \(V=\{1,2\}\); because \(u<v\), necessarily \(u=1\) and \(v=2\), and the queried-edge hypothesis gives \(1\to2\in G\).  Positive definiteness of \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2)\) gives
\[
q_i=e_i^{\top}Qe_i>0,\qquad i=1,2.
\]
Put \(\rho=\sqrt{q_2/q_1}\), which is a strictly positive real number.  For an arbitrary \(a\in\mathbb R\) with \(|a|<\rho\), let
\[
A(a)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\ a&0\end{smallmatrix}\right),
\qquad
D(a)=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2-a^2q_1).
\]
The matrix \(A(a)\) is lower triangular.  Its only possibly nonzero cross-variable entry is \(A(a)_{21}=a\), which is permitted because \(1\to2\in G\); hence it obeys the graph-support restriction in the definition of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  Both diagonal entries of \(A(a)\) vanish, so the stability condition in that definition is
\[
\max_{i\in\{1,2\}}|A(a)_{ii}|=0<1.
\]
Moreover, \(|a|<\rho\) implies \(a^2q_1<q_2\), where multiplication by \(q_1>0\) preserves the strict inequality.  Thus \(D(a)\) is diagonal and
\[
D(a)_{11}=q_1>0,
\qquad
D(a)_{22}=q_2-a^2q_1>0,
\]
so \(D(a)\succ0\).

Direct multiplication gives
\[
A(a)^2=0,
\qquad
A(a)D(a)A(a)^{\top}
=\operatorname{diag}(0,a^2q_1).
\]
Because \(m=3\) and \(B=0\), it follows that
\[
A(a)^m=A(a)^3=0=B
\]
and
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A(a)^rD(a)\bigl(A(a)^r\bigr)^{\top}
=D(a)+A(a)D(a)A(a)^{\top}
=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2)
=Q.
\]
Every condition in the definition of the compatible fiber is therefore satisfied, proving
\[
\bigl(A(a),D(a)\bigr)\in\mathcal S(0,Q;G)
\quad\text{for every }a\in(-\rho,\rho).
\]

For this compatible pair, \(A(a)_{21}=a\) and \(A(a)_{22}=0\).  The definition of the queried direct transfer therefore yields, for every \(z\in\mathbb T\),
\[
h_{12}^{(a)}(z)
=\frac{A(a)_{21}z}{1-A(a)_{22}z}
=az.
\]
Since \(|z|=1\) entails \(z\ne0\), distinct values of \(a\) give distinct transfer functions (and distinct transfer values at every \(z\in\mathbb T\)).  Hence the entire open coefficient interval \((-\rho,\rho)\) is attained.

It remains to check that the endpoints are not hidden elsewhere in the compatible fiber.  Let \((\widetilde A,\widetilde D)\in\mathcal S(0,Q;G)\) be arbitrary.  Lower triangularity and diagonal innovations permit the representations
\[
\widetilde A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x&0\\ b&y\end{smallmatrix}\right),
\qquad
\widetilde D=\operatorname{diag}(\delta_1,\delta_2),
\qquad
\delta_1>0,\quad\delta_2>0.
\]
The diagonal entries of \(\widetilde A^3=B=0\) are \(x^3\) and \(y^3\).  Over \(\mathbb R\), \(x^3=y^3=0\) implies \(x=y=0\), whence \(\widetilde A^2=0\).  Applying the coarse-covariance equality in the compatible-fiber definition now gives
\[
Q
=\widetilde D+\widetilde A\widetilde D\widetilde A^{\top}
=\operatorname{diag}(\delta_1,\delta_2+b^2\delta_1).
\]
Equating diagonal entries with \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2)\) yields
\[
\delta_1=q_1,
\qquad
\delta_2=q_2-b^2q_1.
\]
The required strict positivity \(\delta_2>0\) is equivalent to \(|b|<\rho\).  Thus every compatible transfer coefficient is interior, while at \(b=\pm\rho\) one would have \(\delta_2=0\), contradicting \(\widetilde D\succ0\).  The two boundary coefficients are therefore unattained, not merely omitted by the displayed family.

Finally, the effective-input hypothesis puts \(q_1,q_2\in K\).  Because \(K\) is real closed and \(q_2/q_1>0\), its positive square root \(\rho\) lies in \(K\).  The choices
\[
a_-=-\frac{\rho}{2},
\qquad
a_+=\frac{\rho}{2}
\]
are exact, distinct, and interior; their innovation matrices have second diagonal entry \(3q_2/4>0\), and their transfers are respectively \(-\rho z/2\) and \(\rho z/2\).  Consequently the compatible fiber is nonempty and its transfers are not all equal.  Under the output contract in the definition of \(\operatorname{Cert}_{12,3,G}(0,Q)\), neither the incompatibility output nor the common-transfer output can be sound on this instance.  Its ambiguity output must therefore consist of two attained, transfer-distinct witnesses.  The preceding reverse calculation shows that every attained witness has coefficient in \((-\rho,\rho)\), so endpoint-only output is impossible and the witnesses must be interior.

Thus a queried lower edge has an open interval of attained transfer coefficients, and the certificate must return two interior witnesses rather than unattained endpoints.

proofs.proof_tex:
Extend the constructions in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) and \(\mathrm{def{:}certificate}\) to the formal case \(m=1\). By the defining equations of the compatible fiber,
\[
B=A^1=A
\]
and, using \(A^0=I_d\),
\[
Q=\sum_{r=0}^{0}A^rD(A^r)^{\top}=A^0D(A^0)^{\top}=D.
\]
Hence every \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) must equal \((B,Q)\), so the fiber has at most one element. Conversely, substituting \((A,D)=(B,Q)\) into \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) shows that this pair belongs to the fiber exactly when \(B_{ij}=0\) for \(i<j\), \(B_{ij}=0\) for every \(i>j\) with \(j\to i\notin G\), \(\max_i|B_{ii}|<1\), \(Q_{ij}=0\) for \(i\ne j\), and \(Q\succ0\). Thus the fiber is empty if any of these constraints fails and is \(\{(B,Q)\}\) otherwise.

It remains to verify the algorithmic output rather than infer it merely from the cardinality assertion. For \(m=1\), each diagonal root equation used by \(\operatorname{Cert}_{uv,1,G}\) is
\[
a_{ii}=B_{ii},
\]
and therefore has exactly one real branch. Moreover, directly from the declared divided-difference polynomial,
\[
C_1(x,y)=\sum_{r=0}^{0}x^r y^{0-r}=1.
\]
A length-one nondecreasing walk cannot contain two strict increases, so the declared indirect-path remainder satisfies \(R_{vu,1}=0\). The triangular recursion therefore gives, coordinate by coordinate,
\[
B_{vu}=A_{vu}C_1(A_{vv},A_{uu})+R_{vu,1}=A_{vu}.
\]
Thus no divided-difference coordinate is singular and the certificate has only the candidate \(A=B\); the coarse covariance equation then gives only \(D=Q\). The exact compatibility filtering in \(\mathrm{def{:}certificate}\) rejects this candidate and returns incompatibility precisely when the fiber is empty, and otherwise accepts it. In the latter case the two-copy transfer-inequality system is infeasible because both copies equal \((B,Q)\), so the common-transfer branch of the certificate returns
\[
h_{uv}(z)=\frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}=\frac{B_{vu}z}{1-B_{vv}z}.
\]
Finally, compatibility gives \(|B_{vv}|<1\); since \(|z|=1\), one has \(|B_{vv}z|<1\), whence \(1-B_{vv}z\ne0\). The displayed rational transfer is therefore well defined on \(\mathbb T\), completing the claimed unaliased reduction.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
Under the formal specialization of the displayed constructions to \(m=1\), one has \(B=A\) and \(Q=D\). Consequently, \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) is empty when \((B,Q)\) violates any fine-grid compatibility constraint and otherwise equals the singleton \(\{(B,Q)\}\). Accordingly, on an admissible exact input the certificate returns incompatibility in the first case, while in the second case it returns the unique transfer
\[
h_{uv}(z)=\frac{B_{vu}z}{1-B_{vv}z},
\]
which is the standard unaliased direct process transfer.
